editorials.title: Visits set stage for a weighty season of diplomatic dialogues
editorials.passage: A season of consequential diplomacy appears to be on hand as signals emerge from several directions at once. The unannounced visit of CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow, where he held talks with Russian intelligence officials is perhaps the brightest flare. The Kremlin confirmed the meetings while noting that Ratcliffe did not meet President Vladimir Putin. That distinction may be less important than the visit itself. At a time when US-Russia relations remain deeply strained, the fact that the CIA chief travelled to Moscow is significant. As the Kremlin noted, intelligence channels often remain open even during the darkest phases of diplomacy. India, meanwhile, is moving on multiple diplomatic tracks. External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar’s visit to Moscow included a meeting with Putin and the delivery of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s personal message. More significantly, Jaishankar said Modi looks forward to meeting Putin at the forthcoming Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan this month-end and to welcoming him to India for the BRICS summit soon after.Then there is the China channel. National Security Adviser Ajit Doval’s talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi focused on border issues and the broader bilateral relationship. Beijing described the discussions as comprehensive, candid and friendly, while both sides announced steps to manage the border more effectively as they work towards a political solution..Coming ahead of a likely visit by President Xi Jinping—and amid continuing efforts to stabilise India-China relations after years of border tensions—the timing is difficult to ignore. Taken together, these developments suggest that the diplomatic calendar is indeed becoming consequential.The forthcoming SCO and BRICS summits offer platforms where countries that may disagree sharply on major geopolitical questions can still meet, talk, test possibilities and build consensus. In a fragmented international system, simply keeping these channels open matters.For India, this is a particularly important. New Delhi has consistently pursued strategic autonomy maintaining strong ties with Washington and Moscow while simultaneously managing a difficult but important relationship with Beijing. And across the Global South, countries are asserting greater agency in shaping a more diverse and genuinely multipolar international order.Amid this change, the willingness to talk creates space for de-escalation and greater understanding. Dialogue creates possibilities that confrontation cannot. editorials.title: Law imperils green cover in Garden City Bengaluru
editorials.passage: Bengaluru's civil society’s efforts to protect the city’s two lungs—Lalbagh and Cubbon Park, spread over 200 acres each—appear to be undermined with the passing of the Karnataka Government Parks (Preservation) Amendment Bill. It empowers the government to ‘alienate’ 5 percent of land in public parks for infrastructure projects in ‘public interest’, allowing the authorities to lease, sell, gift, exchange, mortgage or transfer the carved out land, though only to government departments and statutory bodies. The Bill was passed without debate while the opposition was busy creating a ruckus for the resignation of minister B Nagendra over a scam; the BJP and JDS are now denouncing it as serving the Congress government’s real estate interests. There was no such provision under the Karnataka Parks, Playfields and Open Spaces (Preservation and Regulation) Act, 1985.The amendment’s timing raises questions. It could pave the way for takeover of land in Lalbagh—six acres temporarily and one acre permanently—for Chief Minister D K Shivakumar’s pet tunnel project. The 17-km tunnel connecting Hebbal in north Bengaluru to Silk Board in the south will cut through Lalbagh. This has raised the hackles of ecologists, who have been demanding an environmental impact study before the project is finalised. Their main concern is how tunnelling will impact Lalbagh rock, a 3.4-billion-year-old peninsular gneiss formation that has been declared a National Geological Monument, apart from the loss of tree cover. The government claims the road will bypass the rock. .The project has been challenged in the Karnataka High Court for violating the Government Parks (Preservation) Act; the amendment circumvents any debate in court. While checks are in place by way of assessments by official committees, the change opens up space for misuse. It is also risking parks across the state and opening the gates for further loss of green cover—the state capital’s cover has plunged from 70 percent in the 1970s to 3 percent. For the government, 5 percent of Cubbon Park or Lalbagh would mean 10 acres at its disposal. It’s earlier attempt to put up a 10-storey structure in Cubbon Park was averted by alert citizens. editorials.title: Quick Take | Himalayan fury
editorials.passage: There’s no denying that the image of a massive body of water rushing to find level—like the videos that emerged from northern Nepal’s Rasuwa area on Wednesday—terrifies us. The flash flood pummelling down the Bhote Koshi river north of Kathmandu, triggered by an earthquake that set off an avalanche, has claimed at least 95 lives, with 600 others including 105 Indian nationals reported missing. While the government rushes relief to the neighbouring country, we must also look closer at the continuing flood devastation in Assam, where the Brahmaputra’s level is expected to rise again. With at least 107 deaths and 1.5 lakh people displaced, it’s a matter deserving national attention. editorials.title: A waiting economy
editorials.passage:
The youth protest brought attention to India’s job situation and to a by-now familiar statistic: around 40% of graduates aged between 15-25 years are unemployed. The number is alarming. The demonstrations that spread across the country and converged in New Delhi began with anger over examination irregularities and accountability demands over such leakages. But underneath these grievances lies a larger economic problem: millions of young Indians are spending some of their most productive years preparing, applying, waiting and trying again for a limited number of entries into secure employment. This economic phenomenon, visible in the protests, precedes the jobs question. It is a relatively less-discussed cost to the economy in terms of lost productivity and foregone output. There is little we know about the economic cost of this waiting or waithood , to put it succinctly.

India’s examination pipeline — the gateway to a decent work life — takes away some of the most productive years of a generation. Young persons preparing for a competitive examination — NEET, CUET, JEE, UPSC or any other — do not seem unemployed in the conventional sense. They may be studying, enrolled in coaching, taking exams, or filling out applications. Or they may be waiting for a result, a recruitment notification, a court decision or another attempt.

In economic terms, much of this is time spent outside productive employment. This time out has an opportunity cost. Graduates who spend two-three additional years preparing for a government job or professional entrance exams usually earn little or nothing. They are neither gaining work experience, nor acquiring any job-specific skill. They remain financially dependent on their families and delay decisions that typically follow stable employment — the first steps towards an independent life like moving out, buying or renting a home, forming a household, marrying, or simply becoming financially independent. This cost is not only borne by the graduates but also by the households that support them. And ultimately, it is borne by the economy that has invested in their education but is not fully exploiting their productive capacity.

This is the hidden economic cost of making young people wait. Indian households now finance this waithood at a gigantic scale, roughly equivalent to the test-preparation market that by now is a mid-sized industry — valued somewhere between $12-$15 billion and 9%-15% growth on a compounded annual basis — according to different estimates. JEE and NEET together account for nearly 70% of the undergraduate entrance-exam expenditure, which directly devolves upon individual households. This is not discretionary spending but indicates that the money that households would otherwise save or spend on other goods and services or finance the economic mobility the exam itself is meant to deliver but which, instead, is being staked repeatedly against narrowing odds.

The competitive exam system has thus become a labour market queue. Delayed entry into the workforce does not merely postpone earnings: it permanently lowers them. This is the least understood and examined cost of India’s waiting economy. The economist, Kunal Mangal, provides some remarkably clean evidence with his study of a partial, public-sector recruitment freeze in Tamil Nadu between 2001 and 2006. The pause on a subset of government jobs made the remaining vacancies more competitive. Aspirants, however, responded exactly as they do today — worked less to prepare more. A decade later, the affected set of people had lower employment rates, had delayed forming their own households, and displayed lower earning capacity compared to those candidates who had not faced the freeze, while the older family members compensated by extending their own retirement. This finding is an eye-opener and mirrors the broad trend amongst people who enter the workforce late or during a downturn — it is explained by the fact that earlier years in a career have the steepest wage growth in the work-life cycle. So losing out on these years does not just postpone earnings but permanently lowers them. A candidate who enters the workforce at 27 instead of 22 is not only five years behind but also may never fully catch up, according to research evidence.

The broader economic implication is that the real cost is not private. It is macroeconomic — and it is not visible. This is what makes the youth protests a genuine economic story, not just a social one. If even a fraction of India’s exam-aspirant segment — possibly several million people at any given time if we added together the UPSC, JEE, NEET, SSC, banking and state-service streams amongst important ones — were to enter the productive workforce, let’s say the private sector, two to three years earlier than they do at present, the gains would show up in every macroeconomic channel — for example, additional years of formal-sector output, additional consumption, additional direct-tax revenue (giving a much-needed boost to the country’s tax base) and, most important of all, additional human-capital accumulation of the right kind, such as on-the-job skills that are highly valued.

Do we know the aggregate costs of waiting in the labour market queue? A meaningful quantification is not known of at this point. However, even conservative, back-of-the-envelope calculations would place the annual output foregone as a result of queuing at a significant portion of total GDP. It is a figure worthy of official scrutiny for comprehensive understanding and policy formulation. A cost that is presumably large should not stay uncalculated. At present, the cost to the economy is invisible — someone in year three of NEET coaching is not counted as unemployed and is often not clearly categorised as ‘in education’ either; labour force surveys have no clean ‘aspirant’ group.

There is no doubt that the youth protests have shown that India’s growth model is not creating enough jobs. However, a more tractable problem occurs earlier in the pipeline. Unlimited attempts, decade-wide age windows, and artificially scarce seats fail to resolve the jobs shortage and, instead, actively manufacture a second one much before any job is at stake. That is a self-inflicted policy design problem, not of the business cycle and, unlike the job scarcity, is more easily addressed than the efforts required to increase the employment-intensity of India’s growth.

Renu Kohli is Senior Fellow, Centre for Social and Economic Progress, New Delhi. Views are personal

editorials.title: Careless whispers as capital
editorials.passage:
Miryam, if social media and some international newspapers are to be believed, is now a rich woman. In Colombia, where, according to some estimates, the average monthly income of women varies between 400 and 430 US dollars, Miryam — she hails from the agrarian province of Armenia — is today the proud owner of two mansions. But more than Miryam’s wealth, it is her path to prosperity that has shone the spotlight on her. Miryam did not strike gold, or oil. Her capital, interestingly, is chisme — gossip in Spanish. The lady monetises the information she gathers — Miss Marple-like? — her ears perpetually pricked at bits of buzz being churned out in her neighbourhood. Her methodology also involves teasing nuggets out of unsuspecting loose tongues during board games or in social gatherings. This ‘data’ are recorded diligently — in notebooks — and are tested for veracity: Miryam’s house apparently has a bulletin board bearing evidence in the form of photographs and notes. The price of information varies. The benign ones sell for, if the claims are to believed, between 5,000 and 10,000 pesos. But a sensitive matter, such as adultery, can pinch the client’s pocket. Miryam has said that she had once earned 700,000 pesos trading tittle-tattle for one such indiscretion.

Miryam has been praised for her business acumen; she has also been criticised for being an unethical busy­body. This inflamed debate, however, misses a larger point. Miryam’s ‘accomplishment’ should serve as an occasion to revisit the fascinating etymological, social, economic and cultural underpinnings of gossip.

Gossip’s antecedents can be traced back to the earliest epochs of recorded history. In Scandal: A Scurrilous History of Gossip , Roger Wilkes informs readers of a cuneiform Mesopotamian tablet from 1500 BCE whispering about a mayor’s affair with a married woman. But in medieval England, as Silvia Federici has pointed out in her work, Witches, Witch-hunting, and Women , gossip was synonymous with female companionship and solidarity, indicative of collective labour and its resultant emotional bonds among women. One of the sources that Federici cites as evidence of gossip’s glue in creating guilds of self-assertive women is a satirical — hilarious — mystery play of the Chester Cycle in which Noah’s wife refuses to leave with her husband even as the waters rise around them “unless she is allowed to take her gossips with her”. In the physical altercation that follows, Noah is beaten to a pulp by his formidable Missus. But by the 16th century, under a ferocious pushback against women’s autonomy by patriarchy and complicit institutions, such as the church, the meaning of gossip, Federici notes, had begun to get transformed — distorted — to indicate idle, amoral banter.

Yet science disproves gossip’s supposed gendered skin. Researchers from the University of California, Riverside had once made 467 adults, men and women, wear electronic recorders over a few days and, then, analysed the content of their conversations during that time period. The findings, which were published in Social Psychological and Personality Science , a peer-reviewed journal, revealed that not only had the majority of respondents of both genders indulged in gossip but also women, not men, had participated in gupshup that was ‘neutral’ — benign in research parlance.

Gossip gave Miryam an economic lifeline. But can chitchat serve as capital for altruistic, as opposed to personal, gain? The data on gossip as a force for collective economic well-being are revealing. Consider the set of experiments conducted by Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo, Arun G. Chandrasekhar and Matthew O. Jackson in Karnataka and Haryana, respectively, the outcomes of which were published in The Review of Economic Studies . Broadly speaking, their findings suggest that gossip can function as a critical node for disseminating information to meet welfare goals: villages that could identify effective transmitters of important information, their experiment revealed, registered better vaccination rates among children.

And those who use the pulpit of the media to denounce prattle would perhaps do well to remember the productive relationship between the media and rumour mills. Roger Wilkes demonstrates how gossip’s potential, albeit as a moralising tool, coincided with the explosion of print culture. Indeed, the sensational divorce of Lady Colin Campbell — George Bernard Shaw’s muse — may not have taken place had it not been for a salacious newspaper article that fanned the flames. This combustible partnership between the media and hearsay was to be cemented in the years to come in the form of gossip and celebrity columns. Television and, now, digital media have been worthy successors in this regard. Literature’s fraternising with gossip is of note too. The content of Gertrude Stein’s The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas , an exposition on — exposé of — the avant-garde ambience in Paris, has been described by critics as nothing but fruity gossip about literary and art titans. But literature and art have also shown that prurience need not be gossip’s only moorings: its uses as a form of social commentary are not to be undermined. There are handy examples of this from domestic shores: Kaliprasanna Singha’s imaginative use of banter from Calcutta’s streets to reveal, among other things, the hollow pomposity and the pettiness of the affluent as well as rising class tensions in Hutom Pnyachar Naksha is one obvious example; Kalighat pats are another.

This is not to suggest that gossip is foolproof ethically. Its power and its perversity stem from a shared grey area: the fruition of targeted, toxic tidbits requires the absence of the defendant and an unprejudiced adjudicator. In other words, the non-availability of an instrument of authenticity, of truth — the foundational principle of jurisprudence — is a precondition for gossip’s survival and evolution. Gossip’s modern avatars, spread with lightning speed by social media platforms and algorithm-fed technology in post-truth polities, remain equally dependent on such an absence, indeed weakening, of cultures of accuracy, credibility and, above all, truth-telling.

Where does all this leave Miryam?

She may be a successful entrepreneur; she may be unethical. But mostly, the lady is a mirror, reflecting humanity’s meandering engagement with careless whispers.

editorials.title: Tricky balance
editorials.passage:
India will host the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi next month under India’s presidency. BRICS has become central to the contest over the future of the international order. India’s approach has been a balancing act: strengthening the voice of the Global South without allowing BRICS to become an explicitly anti-Western coalition. The theme of India’s presidency — “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability” — captures this ambition. The emphasis on a “humanity-first” agenda intends to make BRICS an instrument of practical economic cooperation rather than an arena for geopolitical polarisation.

Disruptions, from the pandemic and supply-chain shocks to sanctions and geopolitical conflicts, have underscored the vulnerabilities of emerging economies. India is thus likely to push for more diversified and shock-resistant supply chains, particularly in critical minerals, agriculture, energy, and manufacturing. Innovation and digital integration provide another area where India has considerable diplomatic capital to deploy, especially its experience with Digital Public Infrastructure. The third pillar, cooperation, is inseparable from India’s longstanding advocacy of reformed multilateralism. New Delhi has long argued that institutions such as the United Nations, the International Monetary Fund, and World Bank no longer reflect the distribution of global economic and political power. BRICS gives India a platform to press for greater representation and agency for the Global South.

India seeks a more representative and responsive system while retaining an open, rules-based international framework. This distinguishes New Delhi’s approach from members that may view BRICS as a challenge to Western dominance. The trick for India will be to maintain its reformist orientation amid the divergent political preferences of an increasingly heterogeneous membership.

Several outcomes could give India’s agenda greater credibility. BRICS members could seek to expand local-currency trade and payment mechanisms, reducing transaction costs and de­pendence on third-country financial infrastructu­re. The New Deve­lopment Bank could play a larger role through increased local-currency lending for infrastructure and sustainable development projects. Supply-chain cooperation may prove particularly consequential. Coordination on critical minerals, food production, energy security, and manufacturing could move BRICS beyond declaratory diplomacy. Yet translating these ambitions into common policy will be difficult.

The principal challenge is that BRICS is not a strategically coherent bloc. Its members differ sharply — Russia and Iran, for instance, have an adversarial relationship with the West. New Delhi will thus have to resist pressures to turn BRICS into an explicitly anti-West platform while preserving its credibility within the group. The China question is even more complicated. India and China can cooperate on questions of Global South representation and economic reform while remaining strategic competitors. The durability of India’s BRICS diplomacy will depend, in part, on its ability to compartmentalise these competing interests.

The expansion of BRICS adds to the complexity. A larger membership enhances the grouping’s representational weight but makes consensus harder. Recent tensions between Iran and the United Arab Emirates are a case in point. Their opposing positions during the escalating regional confrontation contributed to divisions at the May BRICS foreign ministers’ meeting in New Delhi, which ended without a joint communiqué. This presents a particular challenge for India because it has important strategic and economic interests in maintaining productive relations with both Tehran and Abu Dhabi. India will have to ensure that intra-group conflicts do not turn BRICS into an arena for the projection of regional rivalries.

India’s fourth BRICS presidency is thus significant for New Delhi to demonstrate that strategic autonomy remains compatible with effective multilateralism. The success of the 2026 presidency will depend on whether India can convert BRICS from a forum of divergent geopolitical interests into a platform for concrete cooperation and, in doing so, give substance to its claim to speak for a more representative Global South.

Harsh V. Pant is Vice-President for Studies and Foreign Policy, Observer Research Foundation

editorials.title: Mind the gap: Editorial on India’s education and jobs crisis
editorials.passage:
NITI Aayog’s latest findings indicate a waste of India’s demographic dividend. Unemployment among India’s graduates is four times the national average of 3.2% — 13% overall and an even higher 20.4% for women. Worse, only 8.25% of graduates get jobs aligned to their qualifications. More than half of employed graduates are concentrated in elementary or semi-skilled occupations. This exposes not only a grave failure in creating sufficient skilled employment but also shortcomings in higher education. Data show that the curricula of bachelor’s courses remain generic, theoretical, outdated and poorly connected to employment. Around 80% of higher-education students cite inadequate practical experience and industry exposure while 47% of formal workers identify the absence of internships as a major obstacle to finding work. Even those who do manage to find work suffer. Graduates without supplementary training earn an average starting salary of Rs 22,000 a month against Rs 29,000 for those with additional skills. A sizeable number of students who want to become entrepreneurs have no idea how to go about it. The scale of the crisis is evident in the widespread youth protests which may have electoral implications.

Educational challenges, though, are just one aspect of the problem. The shortage of skilled jobs is equally severe. India still employs 43% of its workers in agriculture and barely 12.1% in manufacturing. Recent employment growth remains heavily dependent on self-employment and unpaid family labour. There is also a paucity of private investment in job creation; this is important since public-sector recruitment alone cannot absorb India’s growing workforce. Ameliorative steps are necessary. Can China serve as a useful template, especially in education? Between 2021 and 2025, its universities closed or suspended 12,200 undergraduate programmes, introduced 10,200 and revised more than 30% of programmes, while its vocational-education law formally embedded apprenticeships and enterprise participation. The NITI Aayog report has underlined some reforms. India needs regular curriculum audits, published course-level placement and wage records, paid apprenticeships with enforceable standards, well-equipped public colleges, trained vocational teachers and industry partnerships tied to measurable employment outcomes. These reforms must accompany the creation of labour-intensive manufacturing jobs and skilling upgrades. Expanded care services and safe transport for women can help address the gender gap in skilled employment. But none of this will bear fruit unless economic policy creates enough secure and adequately paid work.

editorials.title: Rusted edge: Editorial on the limits of US sanctions against Iran
editorials.passage:
The United States of America has launched its latest economic sanctions targeting Iran and a set of individuals and companies that trade with it as part of Donald Trump’s pressure campaign against Tehran. Mr Trump’s administration has described the moves as an “Economic D-Day” for Tehran, effectively threatening to crush the Iranian economy, at a time when the US’s military campaign is yet to succeed in winning a war that Washington started — unprovoked — six months ago. But even in the latest announcement of sanctions, Mr Trump’s administration appears to have conceded its own limitations. History offers decades of evidence that economic sanctions alone do not force Iran to bend: if anything, they might strengthen the hands of the theocratic regime that has ruled Iran since 1979. In the days before the announcement, Mr Trump’s team had warned that countries that continue to trade with Iran or help it evade the effects of the sanctions would also face harsh penalties from the US, including secondary sanctions. However, thus far, the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has avoided imposing any such punishment on Iran’s trading partners to avoid sending the global financial system into a tailspin.

Implicit in that acknowledgement was a harsh fact: in a deeply-integrated global economy, any step the US takes to damage other countries will have adverse impacts on American consumers. The tariffs imposed by Mr Trump on most nations last year led to inflation in the US, and the war on Iran — resulting in oil price spikes — has raised the price tag of goods in American supermarkets. China, Iran’s largest economic ally, has made clear that it will not comply with US diktats. Russia will almost certainly ignore Mr Trump’s threats too. And they can afford to do so. Decades of economic warfare with the US have made China and Russia develop their financial structures independent of the US-led system. Consequently, the US can only impose limited additional damage to their economies. Generations of Iranians have weathered US sanctions as well. While many may not like their current rulers, they know that their economic crisis is an outcome — in good measure — of American policies. Like his predecessors, Mr Trump is unlikely to win against Iran with economic sanctions.

editorials.title: How Mark Carney’s speeches have become political earthquakes
editorials.passage:
I s it perhaps a sign of the times that Mark Carney , the prime minister of Canada , has become a thrilling orator? A sober banker, he speaks calmly, without many vocal inflections. We expect Canadians to be somewhat flat; even a little boring, and yet Carney has already delivered two remarkable speeches in 2026, and the year is far from over.

The first, at Davos, described a “rupture in the world order”, and “the end of a pleasant fiction”. By that, he meant that the world could no longer depend on the United States to lead the Pax Americana that has largely kept the peace since the end of the second world war.

Carney called for a new “geometry”, allowing nations with shared values to align, and asking middle-sized powers to act together, “because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu”. The United States, traditionally the leader of the west, was not invited to join. Ironically, the speech was delivered on 20 January, the first anniversary of Donald Trump’s second inauguration.

The second speech was a 23-minute address, delivered last Saturday, on 22 August, from a drab government interior in Ottawa. The backdrop was unexceptional, a set of eight Canadian flags, behind a wooden lectern (carved with a maple leaf). There were few rhetorical fireworks. He hardly ever raised his voice.

Yet the speech signaled an earthquake. The news, as widely reported, was that Carney was calling off the trade talks that many expected to resolve or reduce the trade frictions that have been in place ever since Trump slapped his first round of tariffs on Canada, shortly after assuming office.

The failure of the talks surely came as a surprise to Donald Trump, who had announced that a deal was imminent. But as is so often the case, US negotiators had undermined their own position with a series of last-minute power moves, bullying the other side.

In this way, the failure was reminiscent of the way the Trump administration continues to blow up its own peace deals in the Middle East, by adding new conditions at the 11th hour and making false statements afterwards.

Carney’s words stung, too. We expect student activists to speak truth to power; it’s a surprise when a former executive of Goldman Sachs and a former governor of the Bank of England takes on the role.

He is no bomb-thrower. But no one can deny that his message reached the world; nothing confirms it so much as Trump’s frenzied counterattack on social media. Reading the flurry of puerile insults posted on Truth Social was like watching a punch-drunk boxer throwing sprawling haymakers at an adversary too nimble to be hit.

In contrast to Carney’s sober tone, Trump has threatened to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”, called Canadian officials “clowns” , and dismissed Carney as a “governor” instead of a prime minister, as if contemptuous of Canada’s sovereignty. Of course, he laid the groundwork for Canada’s refusal to cave in as soon as he began his second term with a flurry of claims that Canada should become the 51st state.

Unlike the easily-rattled president, the prime minister does not traffic in emotion. His speech was notable for its control of the facts and its unshakable moral authority. This was an economist’s speech, full of accounting.

He began with greetings in both English and French – a subtle reminder that US attempts to strong-arm Canada into relaxing its protections of the French language were never going to work. He promised to update Canadians on the issues behind the talks, then did just that.

Carney furnished precise statistics, revealing just how intertwined the US and Canadian economies are (Canada buys more American cars than the UK, Japan and China combined, and supplies 99% of our natural gas imports). In all of these ways, the speech was like a quaint relic from a different era, when leaders were expected to convey the real truth to their people.

There was also some solid rhetoric, as the speech gained intensity, and grew positively elbows up by the end. Carney referred to “the storm blowing in from Washington”, in a possible reference to the recent forest fires that darkened the relationship some more.

Then he announced that Canada would be seeking to diversify its relationships abroad, in what is obviously a new policy, based on a near-total lack of trust in the United States, a nation that blusters so unpredictably on the world stage that it is as if “its signature was written in pencil”.

Canada is far from perfect; it has faced a threat of secession from Francophone Quebec for generations; and there are new murmurs of secession-talk in Alberta. For centuries it was a “dominion” of the British empire, and not clearly a sovereign nation. But its graveyards are filled with tens of thousands of soldiers who served in the first and second world wars; Canadian resolve should never be underestimated.

The loser in this negotiation is, of course, the United States. It’s not just the financial benefits that would have accrued from a successful deal (and the political benefits that would have come to Republicans in swing states that neighbor Canada, such as Michigan and Maine).

It’s a much larger loss than that. As with the proposed case to annex Greenland, this was an entirely avoidable own goal that will damage US interests for a generation, as Canada seeks new relationships. As Carney said: “We are masters in our own home and the partner of choice abroad.” He added: “We have been under no illusions. We recognized from the start that America has changed.”

Those words should alarm all Americans. We hear a great deal about the “special relationship” that links the UK and the US, and it has often been very important, as it was in the second world war.

But the US-Canadian friendship is the healthiest foreign relationship the United States has ever enjoyed. Our economies are deeply connected; as are our militaries (and specifically the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or Norad, which has protected both nations from a Russian attack since 1958).

We share the longest land border between two countries in the world, 5,525 miles long, and in most of our history we have barely worried about it. A huge state, Alaska, cannot be reached by land without going through Canada. In short, we need each other.

And in general, we like each other. At least we did. But in 2025, Canadian tourism in the US declined 25%, and US businesses are feeling it.

The rapid disintegration of the friendship should hardly come as a surprise to any who have followed the rapid erosion of American standing in the world. But Carney’s words spelled out the why and how of this erosion with more clarity that we have heard in a long time. While Canada was proposing “long-term partnerships”, US negotiators were offering “short-term transactions”.

That is not a strong foundation for a world order. While continuing to fantasize about Greenland, and raining down insults on Nato members, we are in danger of losing a much more important ally, close to home.

Carney’s final words left little doubt about the path Canada has chosen. The words are beautiful, if tragic:

“Canada is becoming stronger and less dependent on America. We are already giving ourselves more than they can take away. And we are just getting started. Canadians don’t submit to the weather – we thrive in it. We don’t wait to see which way the wind is blowing. Or surrender ourselves to the waves to be storm-tossed by events. We set our own course. We make our own weather.”

Ted Widmer, a former White House speechwriter, is the editor of American Speeches, and the recently published The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text, both published by the Library of America

editorials.title: With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition
editorials.passage:
N ow is the twilight of Donald Trump’s supremacy. The US is still the richest and most heavily armed nation on Earth. That status is secure. The current president, contemptuous of law and indulged in lawlessness by a supine Congress, enjoys even greater power than the constitution allows.

With those advantages it takes a special talent for incompetence to look as thwarted and impotent as Trump does with more than two years of his second term still to run.

History will record the war against Iran as a turning point in the fortunes of the current US administration and a grievous wound to national prestige.

Pumped with hubris after the audacious military operation to kidnap Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro , Trump believed an equally brisk triumph was available in the Middle East. The Tehran regime would be decapitated. The country’s hydrocarbon resources would then be available for US exploitation.

Six months later, Iran is controlled by a new generation of hardliners. Emboldened by resilience under US and Israeli bombardment, they demand financial concessions from Washington as the price for peace – reparations and a right to toll the strait of Hormuz.

The war is not over, it has just turned cold. Trump believes Iran’s fragile economy is close to collapse. He threatens to push it over the brink with “D-day” sanctions . The metaphor of second world war amphibious assault is supposed to make yet another round of financial coercion succeed where past embargos have failed.

It is true that ordinary Iranians are suffering terrible privations, but repression limits their capacity to translate discontent into demands for political change. By contrast, US consumers, aggrieved by the inflationary consequences of the war , and confused about its purpose , get to express their unhappiness in midterm elections in November.

The calculation in Tehran is that American tolerance for economic pain is low enough that Trump will be forced to blink first. It is a reasonable assumption: the need to declare mission accomplished to a domestic audience – even on terms that amount to defeat by any objective measure – drives an impatient president’s actions more than long-term strategy.

If sanctions fail, diplomatic climbdown is the only remaining move. The Pentagon couldn’t revert to the all-out military option even if Trump ordered it, because Operation Epic Fury burned too much of the national munitions stockpile .

This is where an asymmetry of cost and capability comes into play. Iran can frighten ships out of the Gulf with a few mines. It can harry neighbouring states with drones knocked together for less than $50,000 and dispatched from mobile launchers that are hard to target. The Patriot interceptors that protect US forces and their allies in the region cost $4-5m apiece. (More than 1,500 Patriots are thought have been fired in the war so far , leaving fewer than 830 in the US inventory.)

That depletion has global repercussions, most pressingly in Ukraine where top-end US interceptors are essential for shielding civilians from Russia’s most sophisticated ballistic missiles.

Trump’s attitude to that conflict has evolved from craven pro-Kremlin partisanship and an assumption of inevitable Russian victory to grudging respect for Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s fortitude and ingenuity in proving that assumption wrong. But the shift is not stable. It depends on undertakings by Nato’s European members to cover the cost of arming Kyiv.

If Trump had used normal diplomacy to cajole European democracies into financing the defence of their eastern flank , it would count as a foreign policy success – rebalancing the relationship to both sides’ benefit. But he did it with credulous admiration for Vladimir Putin and deranged demands for territory in Greenland. As a result, the European drive to autonomy looks less like burden-sharing and more like a hedge against American perfidy.

It isn’t just Europe where US allies feel burned. Gulf states that found themselves on the frontline of Iranian retaliation in a war they didn’t start or want, expected a more reliable umbrella of protection. They feel unrewarded for their decades of service, hosting US military bases and functioning as proxies for American interests in the region.

Last week Trump abruptly cut short a joint military exercise with South Korea – a loyal Asian partner to the US. A rational explanation, and the one preferred by Seoul, was that US forces were overstretched by their Middle Eastern entanglement. Trump framed it instead as an amicable gesture towards North Korean tyrant Kim Jong-un, whose regime he judged to be “unthreatening and respectful”.

Such civility, lavished on a monstrous dictatorship, is withheld from Canada , a benign democracy. Trump dismisses his northern neighbour as an economic freeloader, barely even a proper country; a mislabelled territory that should be the 51st US state.

Unsurprisingly, that attitude sours relations. Canadian prime minister Mark Carney pulled out of trade talks last weekend, citing unreasonable last-minute demands from US negotiators. Trump responded with punitive tariffs, to which the Canadians promise “dollar-for-dollar” retaliation.

The smaller economy is likely to suffer more from a trade war. But for Carney the cost in reduced commerce had to be weighed against the political damage he may incur if seen to capitulate to Trump’s bullying . He knows the US president takes concessions as an invitation to come back with yet more demands. He also knows that November’s midterm elections are likely to flip the House of Representatives to Democratic party control, and possibly the Senate too.

Trump cannot be chastened by unwelcome election results. He would rather deny their validity. But irrefutable evidence of failure at the ballot box may at least stir some Republicans out of stupefied obedience to a commander-in-chief whose way of governing has made their party less popular and left their country friendless.

Even if the constitutional mechanisms that are supposed to keep a president in check are only partly rehabilitated, the spell of impunity is broken. The cult of personality that once made Trump look like an irrepressible force of nature has shrunk to a sycophantic sect. An administration that styled itself as a national revolution looks more like a kleptocratic junta, using the privileges of office to pilfer what it can as the clock runs down.

The president still has followers across the country. A hardcore bring unshakable devotion to the cause. But even some of them can surely sense the decay of purpose and whiff of panic in a man running out of ammunition.

Trump’s reign is far from over. With his hands on the levers of American power he can still do a lot of damage. But the rest of the world has learned to read his lurches, anticipate his spasms, manoeuvre around him. The phase of deference is past. Now is the time of planning for whatever comes next in the dimming light of a waning star.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: My home state is set to hand a breakthrough to the German far right. It’s a disaster decades in the making
editorials.passage:
I t was in the summer of 2004 that I stopped understanding my own people. I was standing on a sweltering market square in Aschersleben, the town where I was born, picturesquely situated on the northern edge of the Harz mountains. A large crowd of angry people had gathered in front of a stage to protest about the welfare reforms (or, as many saw them, welfare cuts) introduced by the Social Democratic-Green coalition government under chancellor Gerhard Schröder. They chanted “We are the people!”, waved handpainted placards and seemed utterly beside themselves.

I had gone to secondary school nearby, volunteered at the local hospital and interned at the local newspaper: I knew this place. And yet I found myself bewildered. What, exactly, did these deeply aggrieved people want – standing on a freshly renovated, almost idyllic market square? Weren’t things going reasonably well for them? Where did this burning resentment toward the west come from? Wasn’t the east-west divide supposed to be disappearing by now?

More than two decades later, similar questions can once again be asked.

Eastern Germany is facing a blue wave – or rather, a blue flood. In the state election in Saxony-Anhalt on 6 September, the far right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), whose party colour is blue, is almost certain to emerge as the largest party . Opinion polls consistently place the AfD above 40% , while the governing Christian Democrats (CDU) trail on around 23%. The Left party, once dominant in the east, has fallen to just 13%, while the Social Democrats (SPD) are struggling to clear the 5% electoral threshold.

Should only three or four parties enter parliament, the way would be open for Germany’s first-ever state government led solely by the AfD. The established parties would find themselves stranded on the other side of the much-invoked political “ firewall ” against cooperation with the far right – and, for the first time since 1945, a party containing openly extremist factions would hold governmental power in a German federal state.

The AfD would exercise considerable authority over policing, the judiciary, education and cultural affairs – areas that the party seeks fundamentally to “re-nationalise”, for example by reducing funding for memorial sites commemorating Nazi crimes and revising school curriculums to place greater emphasis on what it regards as the achievements of German history.

For me – and, I suspect, for many East Germans who have left their homeland – the rise of these developments did not come as such a surprise. During my infrequent visits home over the past 10 years, it was palpable that something fundamental was shifting.

When we celebrated the milestone birthday of an old school friend in early 2024, a group of longtime friends flew in to spend a cold January weekend together in Hettstedt. Yet while we cheerfully reminisced about old times, the friend’s family, whom I had always remembered as lively and eager to debate, just sat by, saying almost nothing. I was perplexed. Only later was I told that my friend’s mother – the heart of the family – had forbidden any political discussion. She feared that the guests who had come from afar would be deeply unsettled by how openly people now voiced views that had once been considered taboo.

Saxony-Anhalt has always been a state with a difficult identity. In spite of an extraordinary cultural heritage – it is the home of Martin Luther, George Frideric Händel, Friedrich Nietzsche and the Bauhaus – it lacks a clearly defined regional character. Assembled from various territories of Prussia after its dissolution in 1947, it was abolished during the socialist German Democratic Republic and then re-established after reunification in 1990.

Home to almost 3 million inhabitants at the time, Saxony-Anhalt entered the new era with tremendous optimism – only to suffer a brutal crash landing in the spring of 1991. East Germany’s state-owned industries were to be rapidly privatised by the Treuhand agency in an attempt to make them competitive in a market economy. Yet after decades of central planning and chronic shortages, the socialist combines were scarcely capable of surviving the massive shock produced by the economic and monetary union. Instead of the “flourishing landscapes” that chancellor Helmut Kohl had boldly promised, the whole region entered an unprecedented downward spiral.

The metalworking and chemical industries of southern Saxony-Anhalt were hit particularly hard. During the spring of 1991, hundreds of thousands lost their jobs. Over the rest of the decade, many areas outside the main cities experienced industrial dismantling, mass unemployment and large-scale outmigration.

Younger people, particularly well qualified women, began leaving the region. For my own generation, graduating around the turn of the millennium, moving away appeared to be the only viable path. At the same time, the state steadily withdrew from shrinking rural areas, closing schools and hospitals, relocating courts and police stations. Even the democratic political parties, always much less firmly rooted in eastern than in western Germany, became increasingly invisible.

The echoes of these immense transformations have grown louder once again over the past 35 years. On average, East Germans remain considerably poorer than their western counterparts. They possess significantly less wealth, inherit much less and often face markedly weaker career prospects. A lingering feeling of being “second-class citizens” has become deeply entrenched, extending even to generations born long after German reunification.

I can understand these feelings, and I can understand how the AfD has channelled this pervasive sense of abandonment: through social media , local WhatsApp groups, football clubs and neighbourhood pubs. The anger no longer gathers helplessly on the town square; instead, it has found new energy and vastly greater reach in the digital sphere. And in the polling stations.

What I can’t understand is that the people I grew up among are failing to see how hollow the AfD’s promises are. The slogans this party offers are not solutions. Many of the measures it advocates would only make a grim situation worse. How are businesses or hospitals supposed to recruit the skilled workers they urgently need if the main party simultaneously calls for large-scale “ remigration ”? How can anyone develop a positive vision of the future while at the same time expressing admiration for the Nazi reich or the GDR? It seems a case of suicide out of fear of death, as Bismarck is supposed to have said.

Whether on a sun-drenched market square in the summer of 2004 or at a wintry family celebration in 2024, one thing became unmistakably clear to me: there are neither simple answers nor quick solutions. In Saxony-Anhalt, as elsewhere, the task will be to give people with sometimes very different views and values a genuine sense that they are being included on a shared path toward a common future.

Marcus Böick is assistant professor in modern German history at the University of Cambridge

editorials.title: This is the question Democrats should ask voters in order to win this November
editorials.passage:
T he midterm elections are already upon us, and every Democrat and independent running against a Republican should ask voters the question Ronald Reagan asked on 28 October 1980, at the end of his televised debate against Jimmy Carter: “Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?”

Unless you’re very, very rich, the answer is obviously: “No, I’m worse off.”

Start with his tariffs, which are costing every American household an average of $1,100 annually, according to the Yale Budget Lab . (If you don’t trust Yale, the conservative Tax Foundation estimated last year’s tab to be $1,000 a household.)

Even cleaning supplies and toilet paper are up at least 5% . Household furnishings, up at least 8% . Clothing, up at least 14% . Trump’s tariffs have also increased the costs of big-ticket items such as cars and made it more expensive to build new homes .

Other studies find that the tariffs have added as much as 0.7 and 0.5 percentage points to the consumer price index and the personal consumption expenditures price index, respectively.

Then there’s Trump’s war in Iran, which is driving up energy and food prices, as oil tankers remain stranded in the strait of Hormuz.

The war is costing more at the gas pump – about $670 more a household since the war began. Americans face what the Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers describe as “a worsening utility debt crisis”. The groups wrote in an analysis published last month:

Energy bills have increased three times faster than the rate of inflation while Trump has been president. The national average monthly utility bill reached $280 in early 2026, a 12% increase since the end of 2024, just before the second Trump administration took office.

What’s the Republican response to soaring energy utility prices? Eliminate billions in clean energy subsidies and tilt the scales toward costlier, dirtier fossil fuels.

Also driving up the cost of electricity are AI datacenters. They’re also using up huge amounts of water and creating noise pollution. And who’s been pushing these datacenters? Trump and, before recent backlash , many Republicans.

Trump’s war and the blockage of the strait are also causing fertilizer shortages, which are sending food prices upward. Millions of Americans are now struggling to afford groceries .

Meanwhile, Trump’s huge tax cuts – which mostly benefited big corporations and the super-wealthy – are being paid for, in part, by Republican cuts to Medicaid and Medicare.

Trump announced last month that he is ending Medicare subsidies that have kept drug prices low for seniors; Republican cuts to the Affordable Care Act have deprived millions of Americans of health insurance.

Hell, even Trump’s executive order to divide the measles, mumps, rubella vaccine into three shots instead of one is adding burdens to the typical American family.

As the Republican senator Bill Cassidy said on ABC’s This Week: “This is why the president’s poll numbers are down, because you’ve lost sight of affordability for the parent. You’ve lost sight of the convenience for the American family. You’ve lost sight of that which is driving higher costs in healthcare – for example, more doctor’s visits … for something which has no rationale in science.”

Trump’s obsession with gutting the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has denied Americans billions in foregone rebates and settlements.

The regime spent $464m of taxpayer dollars in a no-bid contract for a special fleet of jets intended to deport immigrants. The planes have almost never been used.

Trump says the US economy is “doing unbelievably from the standpoint of Wall Street”.

Maybe, but most Americans live on Main Street and own few if any shares of stock. The richest 1% holds more than half of the value of stocks listed on US stock exchanges; the richest 10%, 92%. Even including retirement accounts, only 16% of adult Americans have assets exceeding $100,000.

The stock market boom reflects a boom in corporate profits. The pharmaceutical industry , big oil , and other sectors are posting banner earnings. Second quarter earnings for S&P 500 companies are on pace to rise a remarkable 50% year over year , the highest growth rate since the second quarter of 2021.

But average working Americans are struggling to keep their heads above water.

Trump’s comments about the roaring stock market came the same day that new data showed US consumer sentiment dropped in August. Americans’ outlook on the country’s economic conditions have worsened among Republicans as well as among Democrats.

The July jobs report showed the US economy shedding 23,000 jobs, wage growth slowing, and the unemployment rate falling because more people left the workforce.

My humble advice to Democratic candidates in the midterms: don’t be distracted. Don’t take the bait and discuss socialism, “wokeism”, or anything else.

Just ask this simple question: are you better off now than you were before this presidency? And explain how badly Trump and congressional Republicans have shafted average working people.

You’re better off than you were before the start of this presidency only if you’re a major investor in the stock market, a top corporate executive or a beneficiary of Trump’s largesse to his billionaire backers.

But if you’re an average working American, you’re indubitably worse off. Hopefully, you’ll vote your economic interests on 3 November and deposit Trump’s congressional lapdogs into the dustbin of history.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com . His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

editorials.title: The royal commission revealed the breadth of antisemitism in Australia – but key opportunities were missed
editorials.passage:
F rom the moment the prime minister, Anthony Albanese , belatedly announced the royal commission into antisemitism and social cohesion, he clearly wanted the inquiry to be short and tightly focussed. No detours.

By setting Commissioner Virginia Bell a deadline of December 14 – the anniversary of the Bondi massacre – to deliver her report, the PM signalled he had no appetite for surprises or delays.

He seems to have got his wish. The public hearings started in May and wrapped up this week, less than four months in total. Given that there were several intertwined agendas – the spread of antisemitism, a probe into the Bondi massacre, and the impact on social cohesion – it always felt like a race against time.

The commission’s signal achievement has been to hold a mirror to the broader Australian community about the breadth and intensity of hostility that has been directed at Jews since the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023 and the following war in Gaza.

The testimony of lived experience highlighted the extent to which intimidation and victimisation of Jews has permeated virtually every corner of life in this country, from children’s sporting fields to schools and universities, the public service, union movement, arts and entertainment, politics and even the healthcare system.

Much of it grew out of anger at Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza, which does not excuse a single act. But Australian Jews cannot be held responsible for the actions of another government. The repeated rejection of this twisted logic at the hearings has been a crucial takeaway.

Another shocking byproduct was the hatred unleashed towards the witnesses who had been brave enough to step up, identify themselves and give testimony. Just three weeks in, Commissioner Bell said “we have received reports from a number of witnesses concerning a dramatic increase in online hate messages”. This outpouring reinforced the sense that Jews were still fair game.

We had already seen a man outside the commission building in Sydney, during the first week, wearing a T-shirt with a swastika around a Star of David and the words “Antisemitism. Proud to be accused” written on it. In the lead-up to the commission, Jewish communal leaders asserted that antisemitism was being expressed so openly that it had become normalised. The brazenness of the T-shirt incident made it all too clear.

As the hearings moved from individuals to public servants, heads of institutions and civil society organisations, there was a creeping sense that the commission missed a few opportunities to bare its teeth. Yes, the NSW police got a grilling about the Opera House demonstration and security stuff-ups ahead of Bondi, and university chiefs felt the blowtorch over their passivity around the student encampments.

But key gatekeepers of the arts and cultural sector were not called. Noticeably absent were the heads of Creative Australia. It would have been illuminating to hear it explain how it draws the line between funding an individual project and the applicant’s broader activities.

Similarly, I would have liked to hear the Sydney Biennale Board asked about the American DJ who unleashed a rant at the opening night party against the “Zio-Australian-Epstein empire” and declared that “one day we will all be free from the Zionist entity”.

Her performance pointed to a toxic conundrum that often went under the commission’s radar: the intertwining of Zionism and coded language – “Zio” for Zionists – to vilify Jews (and their defenders) over their support for Israel. The subject was not thoroughly interrogated, even after the eminent Indigenous activist Marcia Langton told the Commission last week she had been labelled a “Zio” for expressing her support for Jewish Australians.

Finally, it was also open to Commissioner Bell to call the prime minister to appear. While there are limits to what governments can do to mitigate social bigotry, Albanese, as the leader of this country, had more power than anyone to make a difference.

In the wake of the Bondi massacre on December 14, the PM openly admitted that he could have done more to address rising antisemitism. Was this admission performative or genuine? Either way, it provided the commission with a legitimate reason to call him to spell out exactly what measures and policies he had in mind when he made this admission.

I say this not in the name of blaming him for Bondi, as many in the Jewish community have done, but in the hope he may have shared tangible ideas about how to navigate the future. Australian society, from the top down and the ground up, must leave no stone unturned in eradicating the scourge that has taken hold. Even if that means taking a detour off the straight and narrow.

Michael Visontay is a senior writer at The Jewish Independent

editorials.title: Andy Burnham should rip up our undemocratic first past the post system – even if some in Labour disagree
editorials.passage:
A poll in the Mail on Sunday at the end of June was remarkable. It had not just Reform as low as 21%, but also Labour and the Tories. It was remarkable because it starkly demonstrated the fragmented landscape of the UK’s electoral terrain, as well as the electoral weakness of its main players.

Polls since have varied, not least with the Burnham bounce, but this week’s YouGov voting intention figures put Reform, Labour and the Tories on 23%, 22% and 20% respectively (although it almost no longer matters which exact figure applies to which party). Add in the Greens and the Liberal Democrats on 13% apiece, the SNP dominating Scotland and Plaid Cymru Wales, then Restore UK and independent candidates and you have an unprecedented variety of options laid out before the British electorate.

And all this despite the first past the post (FPTP) electoral system, which has for so long upheld two-party politics. It does so by punishing any party outside the duopoly by refusing to match votes to seats. If this unprecedented level of fragmentation exists in the face of a voting system that coerces people to back only their least bad option, then how diverse would this landscape be if people could vote with their heart and know that their vote really counted?

This now complete mismatch between what voters want and what they get is the root cause of the governing crisis destabilising British politics. Labour won two-thirds of the seats in the Commons in 2024 on just a third of the vote, and its leadership assumed that this result conferred it legitimacy in the eyes of the public. But governments increasingly find that a Commons majority upheld by an unrepresentative voting system is more vulnerable to voter backlash. In this context, support quickly melts away, as Keir Starmer and Morgan McSweeney found out.

If Britain continues under FPTP, then this governing chaos will deepen, and the only beneficiaries will be anti-democratic extremists.

But now there is a golden chance to change all this. Next Wednesday, the representation of the people bill will come before parliament for its final stages. An amendment has been tabled to set up a national commission to look at which system of proportional representation (PR), which does match votes to seats, would best suit our country. It has huge backing in the Commons, in the Labour party and among the public. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, is also a longstanding supporter of electoral reform. The political conditions have never been more favourable to begin making changes to the voting system. What could possibly go wrong?

This: a minority but powerful view within the upper reaches of the Labour party, the cabinet and the party bureaucracy is vehemently opposed to PR and the plural politics of cooperation it demands. According to this tribal view, only Labour, governing alone, can represent the interests of “their voters”. And so it is preferable to lose all power than to share it. Labour winning – however tiny its share of the vote – is more important than democracy working. At best, those with this view may calculate whether PR or FPTP delivers the most Labour MPs, equating self-interest with the national interest.

But all their paternalistic calculations miss the very big point: democracy should not be designed around what is best for Labour – or any party – but around what works best for the country.

Labour’s rearguard reactionaries will try to block the idea of a national commission, water it down or kick it bureaucratically into touch. They will say only the cost of living matters, and that no one brings up PR on the doorstep. But it is precisely our rotten voting system that denies the changes people want, because it prioritises the cautious views of a few swing voters in a few swing seats and impels Labour to pander to them.

The game is over for this old top-down, command-and-control politics. The myth of strong government from FPTP is dead. It is time for change, to do what Willy Brandt, the fabled leader of the German Social Democrats, implored the left to do in 1969, and “dare more democracy”. That means finally embracing multiparty government, and ensuring everyone’s vote is counted equally: it is the only way to end the cycle of chaos.

Radical Manchesterism beats in our prime minister’s heart. There, he made big changes happen by listening to voices beyond Labour and working cross-party to build a long-term consensus to transform a region. Next week, by backing himself and his best instincts on PR, he can transform the country.

Neal Lawson is director of the cross-party campaign organisation Compass

editorials.title: From Kerala to Kargil, ‘Muslim’ ecologies are syncretic and intertwined with the landscape
editorials.passage:
In the vast mangrove delta of the Sundarbans, where the Bengal coast dissolves into tidal rivers and dense forest, survival depends on more than a boat and a net. Before entering the forest to collect honey or cut wood, fishermen and wood-gatherers stop at small shrines along the treeline to invoke Bonbibi, a figure one 19th traveller called a “strange goddess”, believed to be the keeper of the forest.

Bonbibi is, by origin, a Muslim figure. Her legend, interwoven with the tiger god Dakshin Ray and the mediating saint Ghazi Miyan, forms the cosmological grammar of an entire ecosystem: a shared sacred world in which tigers, humans, forest spirits, and Muslim saints negotiate the boundary between the wild and the habitable.

What, exactly, makes this a Muslim ecology? Not the presence of Muslims as such. Hindu, animist, and tribal communities too invoke Bonbibi. What makes it Muslim is that an Islamic idiom – a saint, a sacred genealogy, a moral vocabulary of protection and transgression drawn from Islamic devotional practice – has become one of the registers through which an entire regional community, across religious lines, understands and regulates its relationship with a dangerous and necessary landscape.

This essay is about Muslim ecologies: not environmental knowledge that happens to be held by Muslims, but ecological practice and ethical reasoning in which an Islamic vocabulary does identifiable work: dividing the forest, sanctifying a pond, regulating a water channel, restricting a tree.

The claim here is not that Muslims have a special relationship with nature. It is that, across several regions of India, the vernacular life of Islam – its saints, its legal concepts, its devotional geography – has shaped how land, water and animals are managed. This history has gone almost entirely unrecognised in how India thinks about its environmental past and present.

The story of Bonbibi is best understood not as folklore decoration but as a working cosmology for an unworkable landscape. The Sundarbans are a tidal forest where the line between land and water shifts with every monsoon, where the Bengal tiger is a constant and lethal presence, and where any human entry into the forest interior is, in a quite literal sense, a negotiation with death.

According to the “Bonbibi Johuranama”, a narrative poem that has circulated among fishing and forest-dwelling communities for generations, Bonbibi is sent by God to protect the poor of the forest. She defeats Dakshin Ray, the tiger god and lord of the wild, but does not destroy him: she negotiates. The forest is divided – the deep interior remains the tiger’s domain, while humans may use the margins, provided they enter with humility and seek her blessing first. Ghazi Miyan, the Muslim warrior-saint, witnesses and seals this compact.

This is, in effect, a zoning law expressed as theology. It tells honey-collectors and woodcutters where they may go, on what terms, and what ritual obligations attach to entry – and it does so by fusing an Islamic figure of sainthood with a pre-existing, non-Islamic tiger-deity and forest-spirit complex that long predates the arrival of Islam in Bengal.

The historian Richard Eaton’s account of how Islam became local in Bengal helps explain why this fusion occurred where and how it did. Eaton describes the eastward expansion of Bengali agriculture into forested, sparsely settled tracts of the delta from the 16th century, often led by pirs , Sufi pioneers, who arrived not as conquerors but as forest-clearers. They were granted land by Mughal authorities precisely because they could mobilise local labour and command local legitimacy. These pirs became, in local memory, figures who could ride tigers, command crocodiles, and negotiate with the spirits already understood to inhabit the forest. Sufi shrines functioned, in Eaton’s phrase, as nodes of a “moral ecology” – a cognitive map in which the authority to clear land, the authority to mediate with dangerous animals, and the authority to bless or curse were all held by the same sacred figure.

This is the specific historical mechanism by which an Islamic idiom became a vernacular ecological expression: not through doctrine imposed from above, but through the practical role Sufi pioneers played in the agrarian and ecological frontier of premodern Bengal. The legendary Zindah Ghazi, said to ride tigers, and Khan Jahan, credited with clearing the forests of what is now southwestern Bangladesh by mediating between settlers and the animals and spirits of the land, belong to this same genealogy. Bonbibi is its most enduring popular form – still invoked today by Hindu and Muslim forest-goers alike, in a region where the practical business of staying alive in the mangrove has outlasted, and absorbed, the religious categories that produced it.

A second, more widely distributed pattern concerns the role of Sufi shrines as informal sanctuaries for endangered wildlife. Here the mechanism is different again, and worth spelling out carefully.

At the shrine of Bayazid Bistami in Chittagong, the sacred pond harbours the black soft-shell turtle, among the rarest turtles in the world. Across present-day Bangladesh and Pakistan, researchers have documented similar shrine ponds inhabited by protected fish and crocodiles, which devotees feed and will not harm. The animals are understood to be in some sense the shrine’s own, connected to the saint’s baraka, his spiritual charge, in ways that vary from place to place but that consistently mark the pond and its inhabitants as off-limits to ordinary use.

The mechanism here is not an abstract Islamic teaching about animals in general. It is the specific, local logic of shrine sanctity: a saint’s tomb radiates a kind of protection outward into its immediate environment, and the pond, being physically continuous with the shrine, falls within that radius. Catching the fish or harming the turtle would be to violate the sanctity of the place itself; a transgression against the shrine, which only secondarily, and almost incidentally, has the effect of protecting the species.

The result, in ecological terms, is nonetheless real. Centuries before the language of conservation biology existed, a religious geography of sanctity was functioning as a de facto protected-area network, scattered across the subcontinent wherever Sufi shrines stood near water. The turtle in the shrine pond is not a religious symbol pressed into ecological service. Its survival has depended on the specific local belief that this pond belongs to this saint: a belief that is simultaneously about Islam, and about this place.

A third pattern, in the high-altitude cold desert of Kargil in Ladakh, shows the same Islamic idiom doing different ecological work: not zoning a forest or sanctifying a pond, but regulating water and timber in a landscape where both are catastrophically scarce.

Field studies of Muslim communities in Kargil describe how the cutting of juniper – a slow-growing tree that is ecologically critical for soil stability and fuel in this fragile environment – is restricted through community norms. Participants explicitly describe these norms in the vocabulary of Islamic stewardship: the idea that resources are held in trust and that wasteful or excessive use is a kind of wrongdoing for which one is accountable.

Water in Kargil is distributed through collective irrigation arrangements that draw on a specific principle of Islamic law , that flowing water (as distinct from water that has been collected or stored) cannot be privately owned and access to it is a shared right that no individual can foreclose. This is not a vague spiritual orientation toward nature. This legal concept, drawn from the fiqh tradition, performs a distributive function in the irrigation system: determining who may take water, in what order, and on what basis a dispute over a channel is resolved.

What is striking about Kargil is how precisely the Islamic vocabulary maps onto the ecological problem. A cold desert’s two scarcest resources – wood and water – are governed by, respectively, an ethic of accountable stewardship and a legal doctrine about the non-ownability of flowing water. Neither of these is a generic “Islam is green” claim.

Both are specific doctrinal resources, selected and emphasised because they happen to fit the ecological problem at hand. This is exactly what one would expect when religious vocabulary is used as a regulation by people living with scarcity, rather than being read into their practices after the fact by an outside observer.

A fourth, more diffuse pattern is visible in the way mosques across India took on entirely different built forms depending on region. The multi-pitched terracotta roofs of rural Bengal echo the thatched bamboo-and-mud houses of the delta and shed the region’s heavy monsoon rain.

The sloping tiled roofs of the Malabar coast in Kerala, which use locally available materials, are suited to its different but equally intense rainfall. The tiered wooden forms of Kashmir are built for snow load and for a climate where wood, not stone, was the available building material.

These adaptations are sometimes described simply as evidence of Islam’s capacity to absorb local aesthetic traditions. This is true but understates the point. A roof pitched to shed monsoon rain or built from the timber a forested hill region produces, is a building in working relationship with its climate and its materials.

It is, in a modest but real sense, an ecological adaptation arrived at by communities who needed their houses of worship to survive the same weather as their houses of living. That this adaptation happened differently in Bengal, Kerala and Kashmir – producing three quite different built vocabularies, all recognisably Islamic and local – is itself evidence against any singular “Muslim” relationship to the environment.

What is Muslim here is a set of practices that took shape differently in each place, in dialogue with each place’s ecology. In each of the four cases described – a forest cosmology in Bengal, shrine ponds across the subcontinent, water and timber law in Kargil, and mosque architecture in three regions –what makes the practice “Muslim” is different and specific.

In the Sundarbans, it is a saint-figure and a sacred narrative, of Islamic provenance, that organises a cosmology shared across religious communities. It is Muslim in origin and idiom, but not Muslim in exclusive ownership or practice. In the shrine-ponds, it is the specific logic of Sufi sanctity – the baraka of a tomb extending into its surroundings – that produces a conservation effect as a side-consequence of devotional geography. In Kargil, it is Islamic legal doctrine that supplies the rules of a resource-management system. In mosque architecture, it is the way Islamic religious building, as a category, take on the specific ecological grammar of each region it arrived in.

What unites these cases is not a shared “Islamic environmental ethic” that exists prior to and independent of local context, waiting to be applied. It is rather that Islam in India has also been local and environmental. It arrived in, and took shape within, specific ecological and social landscapes, via specific historical agents: Sufi pioneers in Bengal’s forest frontier, jurists and irrigation communities in Ladakh’s cold desert, builders working with regional materials and climates.

In becoming local, it became, in these instances, ecological. Islamic vocabulary did not arrive as an abstract doctrine and get “applied” to nature in general; it arrived embedded in specific practices of settlement, sanctity, law and building, each of which had to come to terms with a specific landscape.

This also clarifies what this essay is not claiming. It is not claiming that anything done by a person who happens to be Muslim – a Muslim farmer, a Muslim scientist, a Muslim novelist – constitutes “Muslim ecology” simply by virtue of the practitioner’s identity. That would make the category so broad as to be analytically empty and would risk exactly the kind of forced or essentialising move that this framing wants to avoid. The cases above are different in kind. In each, an identifiably Islamic vocabulary, narrative, legal concept or institutional form is doing identifiable work in how land, water, trees, or animals are actually treated.

None of these amounts to a singular claim that Islam determines ecological outcomes, or that Muslim communities are inherently more conservation-minded than others. Region, caste, livelihood and local political economy all matter – often more, in any given instance, than religious identity. The Kargil irrigation system would not function on doctrine alone; it depends on local enforcement, kinship obligation, and the practical fact that everyone in a watershed needs the system to work. The Bonbibi cosmology did not, in itself, prevent the colonial-era and postcolonial destruction of large parts of the Sundarbans mangrove. A cosmology is not a conservation policy, and treating it as a substitute for one would be its own kind of error.

What religious identity does provide, in each of these cases, is a vocabulary: a set of terms – stewardship, sanctity, the non-ownability of flowing water, the moral geography of a saint’s protection – through which ecological relationships can be named, argued about, and handed down.
